The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $K\subseteq M$ be compact, and let $W\subseteq M$ be open with $K\subseteq W$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:M\to [0,1]$ that equals $1$ on an open neighbourhood of $K$ and satisfies $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq W$.

If $M$ is a compact smooth manifold and $f:M\to\mathbb R$ is a Morse function,
then $f$ has only finitely many critical points.

Let $W$ be a compact smooth manifold with boundary and let $f:W\to\mathbb R$ be
a Morse function with finitely many critical points, all interior and none in a
closed neighbourhood $C$ of $\partial W$. Then every $C^\infty$ neighbourhood of
$f$ contains a Morse function $g$ with $g=f$ on $C$, the same critical points and
the same Hessian at each of them, and distinct critical values.

Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, let $p$ be a nondegenerate critical point of
$f$, and let $\lambda$ be the index of $p$. If $n=\dim M$, then there are local
coordinates $(x^1,\dots,x^n)$ centered at $p$ in which

$$f=f(p)-\sum_{i=1}^{\lambda}(x^i)^2+\sum_{i=\lambda+1}^{n}(x^i)^2.$$

For $n=0$, both sums are empty.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth on a boundaryless manifold, $a<b$, and let $K=f^{-1}([a,b])$ be compact with $df\ne0$ on $K$. For any Riemannian metric there is a compactly supported smooth field $Y$ agreeing with $\operatorname{grad}f/\|\operatorname{grad}f\|^2$ near $K$. Its complete flow $\Phi$ satisfies $f(\Phi_t(x))=f(x)+t$ for $x\in K$ and $a-f(x)\le t\le b-f(x)$. Thus every intervening level is reached in exactly its value difference.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:C\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a smooth
isotopy of a finite disjoint union of circles, constant near both ends, and
suppose both end projections under the fixed $\pi$ are regular. Arbitrarily
close to $F$ in the strong smooth topology there is such an isotopy $F'$, equal
to $F$ near the ends, whose projected slices have only these exceptional events:

(i) finitely many ordinary cusps, at distinct times; in a source coordinate
$x$, writing $g(x,t)=\pi F'(x,t)$, each satisfies
$g_x=0$, $\det(g_{xx},g_{xt})\ne0$ and
$\det(g_{xx},g_{xxx})\ne0$;

(ii) the **off-diagonal unordered** double-point locus is a smooth
one-dimensional manifold with boundary in the local-extension sense of
[[def-smooth-chart-atlas-and-structure-on-a-manifold-with-boundary]]; its boundary
consists exactly of the double points at $t=0,1$. Its interior is a manifold
without boundary, and its time projection has only finitely many
nondegenerate critical points, each an ordinary quadratic tangency of two
immersed branches;

(iii) finitely many transverse triple events, with all three pairs of
projected tangents independent, and no quadruple points.

No two exceptional events have the same time. All other slices are regular,
and between exceptional times their decorated diagrams vary by planar isotopy.

Let $F'$ satisfy the general-position conditions of
[[lem-a-smooth-isotopy-of-links-can-be-put-in-general-position]], with
exceptional times $t_1<\cdots<t_N$. Immediately before and after each event,
its regular diagrams differ, up to planar isotopy, by one oriented
Reidemeister move: R1 at an ordinary cusp, R2 at a quadratic double tangency,
and R3 at a transverse triple event. The regular intervals contribute planar
isotopies, and the moves preserve the over/under and orientation data of $F'$.
Consequently the end diagrams are connected by a finite sequence of these moves.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For every oriented link $L$ contained in
$\mathbb R^3$, the directions $u\in S^2$ for which the orthogonal projection
$\pi_u$ is regular are dense in $S^2$. Every such projection has finitely
many double points.

set of $F$ is a null subset of $N$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. 2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.

Assume countable choice. Let $K_0,K_1\subset S^3$ be smooth oriented knots. A smooth oriented knot cobordism from $K_0$ to $K_1$ is a compact smooth properly embedded oriented surface $\Sigma\subset S^3\times[0,1]$ whose boundary is $(-K_0\times\{0\})\sqcup(K_1\times\{1\})$, with product collars at both ends. A **generic movie** for $\Sigma$ is obtained by choosing a generic projection of the slices $S^3\times\{t\}$ to the plane and a Morse height function on $\Sigma$, then recording the oriented link diagram at each regular level. Intermediate regular levels may be links with any finite number of components. After choosing the projection and height generically, the finitely many exceptional levels are isolated and distinct: between them the diagrams change by planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move, and at them the surface height has one nondegenerate minimum (a birth), one nondegenerate maximum (a death), or one index-one critical point (a saddle band move). A movie includes its ordered list of frames and these elementary changes; no claim that two movies of the same cobordism are equivalent is part of this definition.

Assume countable choice. Fix $\infty\in S^3$, put $A=\{\infty\}\times[0,1]$, and identify its complement with $\mathbb R^3\times[0,1]$. Let $S_0,S_1$ be compact smooth oriented link cobordisms disjoint from $A$, with the same fixed boundary parametrizations and product collars. If they are ambient isotopic in $S^3\times[0,1]$ relative to those collars, then their comparison factors into finitely many ambient isotopies supported in the Euclidean complement and finitely many local sheet passages through $A$. Each sheet passage occurs at a regular surface-height point and gives the sweep-around move: in planar movies, a closing arc for a one-interval tangle travels over the tangle to the opposite side and returns underneath, or the inverse, retaining its orientation. All end collars remain fixed. No assertion that a sweep-around is generated by the fifteen Euclidean Carter–Saito moves, or that any homology map respects it, is made.

Assume countable choice. Let two finite generic planar movies represent compact smooth oriented surfaces in $\mathbb R^3\times[0,1]$, with the same parametrized boundary and product collars. It lies on that side of $E$ inside the original ball, apart from the small outside collar of $Q$: the complementary part of the original boundary sphere is connected and lies on the other side, as is checked first near the seam and then by disjointness. Removing the added collar therefore gives a ball region bounded by $E$ and $Q$. No other disk of the system lies inside it, since each has boundary outside $Q$ and is disjoint from $E$.

A degree zero generator has $\chi=k$. If it contains a sphere it vanishes by S. Delete all tori by T, giving $2^t$ times a disk system. For $k=0$, the remaining system is the empty surface. This evaluation respects S and T. It also respects four-tube relations. Indeed components not meeting the four patches give a common factor. If there is a negative Euler characteristic component all four evaluations vanish: a tube on one component lowers its Euler characteristic by two, while a tube merging two components replaces their Euler characteristics by their sum minus two. Even merging with a sphere therefore leaves negative Euler characteristic. If there are at least two spheres, every tube attachment leaves a sphere or merges two spheres to a sphere, so again every evaluation vanishes. With no spheres and only tori, attaching a tube creates a negative Euler characteristic component, and all four values vanish. The remaining case is exactly one sphere and $r$ tori. A tube meeting the sphere in zero, one or two patches has value respectively $0,2^r,2^{r+1}$: in the middle case it merges the sphere with one torus; in the last case it turns the sphere into a torus. Thus its value is $2^r$ times the number of its two patches on the sphere. Both sides of four-tube count each patch once, so their values agree.

Sweep $E$ through this ball region to a fixed disk parallel and very close to $Q$, keeping its boundary collar fixed. In ball coordinates this is the family of disk slices between the two hemispherical faces, stationary in a thin equatorial collar; rounding and a smooth reparametrization make the sweep smooth. Apply the ball-window assertion of [F5] to this actual ball region and its face $Q$, retaining the chosen seam collar; the complementary face is then the opposite hemispherical disk. This supplies the ball coordinates used in the sweep, rather than extending an arbitrary sphere diffeomorphism. The moving part is compactly contained away from the original boundary after deleting its stationary collar. Extend its velocity by the construction of [F3], cut it off before that boundary collar and before the other disks, and use its ambient flow. The velocity is zero where the sweep is stationary, so this extension fixes the entire original boundary and all other disks. Do this for either of the two systems, using the same final parallel disk. Cut off its small boundary ball. The remaining region is again a standard ball by the boundary-ball removal assertion of [F5]. Repeat for the remaining boundary curves. Finite induction identifies both systems with the same successive boundary-parallel disks, and hence with each other. Applying this to the vertical curtain disks proves that the system in step 2.1 is isotopic to $P\times[0,1]$. Thus every degree zero endomorphism is an integral multiple of the identity.

Outside the cylinder cap each of the $k$ prescribed boundary circles by a fixed disjoint once-punctured torus. Such caps exist: take the complementary boundary-parallel disks to the standard curtain system in a second ball and attach to each a tiny handle in its own disjoint neighbourhood. Gluing and applying step 2.2 gives a linear functional on the quotient endomorphism group, since any relation in the cylinder remains the same local relation after closure. A one-term complex has no nonzero homotopies between endomorphisms because the target in cochain degree $-1$ is zero. Its degree zero endomorphism ring is therefore the ring just computed. Its invertible elements are precisely the integers $+1,-1$, since $nm=1$ in $\mathbb Z$ forces that pair of possibilities. A common grading shift leaves these degrees unchanged.
